source.title: Improved Scaling Laws in Linear Regression via Data Reuse
source.authors: Li-Cong Lin; Jing-Feng Wu; Peter L. Bartlett

page_placements.theme: Optimization and reuse can change theoretical training-time exponents

record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling-law analysis to repeated-data training in sketched linear regression and reports theoretical and simulation results; it does not study language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The paper reports scaling results for linear-regression test error under data reuse. Its discussion of LLM scaling laws and results cited from other work are not recorded as rows. The one-pass comparisons in the experiments are included because the authors run and report those comparisons themselves.
record.test_reason: This is a theory paper on M-dimensional Gaussian-sketched linear regression trained by one-pass and multi-pass SGD. It derives population-MSE bounds and checks them with small simulations (d = 10000, M ≤ 1000). It trains no language model or neural network and measures no pretraining cross-entropy, downstream task or other modality. Every version names neural or language-model training, so its results describe a different kind of system. The authors present the work as a theoretical explanation motivated by neural scaling laws. Its findings are recorded under fits_no_version rather than as tests. This is a borderline call: one could argue T3 for V5 (repeated data) or V7 (exponent depends on training regime), but no row measures the system the versions name.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors prove that, under aligned power-law spectra, multi-pass SGD on sketched linear regression achieves a better sample-size scaling than one-pass SGD in data-constrained regimes (exponent (1−b)/b versus (1−b)/a when a>b). Simulations match the predicted exponents. They note the benefit vanishes when a<b<a+1. They name extending the analysis to nonlinear models and cross-entropy loss, the setting relevant to LLMs, as future work.
record.recipe_differences: The paper analyzes Gaussian-sketched linear regression with multi-pass SGD and population mean-squared error, rather than transformer language-model pretraining and held-out cross-entropy.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported rates depend on the spectral exponents and regime, and the comparison changes between one-pass and multi-pass training; the simulations also include Gaussian and non-Gaussian designs and different step-size schedules.

fits_no_version.finding: In sketched linear regression with power-law spectra (a>b>1, N≪M^b), multi-pass SGD reaches excess error Θ(M^(1−b)+N^((1−b)/b)). One-pass SGD reaches Θ(M^(1−b)+N^((1−b)/a)). Simulations fit exponents of −0.33 and −0.36 for multi-pass versus −0.25 for one-pass, and −0.34 versus −0.26 under a non-Gaussian design.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In linear-regression models of scaling laws, data reuse improves the sample-size exponent in data-constrained regimes, so the exponent depends on the training regime.

fits_no_version.finding: When a<b<a+1, multi-pass SGD only matches the one-pass rate. With k = L/N passes, k-pass SGD matches one-pass SGD on kN fresh samples below a threshold number of passes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In linear regression, reused data acts like fresh data up to a pass threshold, and the benefit of reuse depends on the spectral regime.

fits_no_version.finding: Under compute C = L·M, multi-pass SGD reaches the same optimal rate Õ(C^((1−b)/(a+1))) as one-pass SGD. It needs N = O(C^(b/(a+1))) samples rather than O(C^(a/(a+1))). The model-size exponent is about 1−b for both (−0.53 versus −0.50).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In linear regression, data reuse preserves compute-optimal scaling while reducing the required number of unique samples.

record.problems: The theoretical conclusions rely on specified power-law and source assumptions and concern linear regression, not LLM pretraining. Simulation settings are limited (including d = 10000 and 100 samples for error bars); several fitted exponents are presented in figures.
record.rows_left_out: No directly relevant reported results omitted.

untested.parts: No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No parameter/token allocation for language models; only an M-versus-SGD-steps split in linear regression.
No image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer results for neural models; linear regression only.
No published-law or fitting-choice comparison for neural models.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests/T3' with V5 and V7 'supports' is overturned because the system is not a neural or language model. If reviewers accept simplified theoretical models as bearing on V5 (repeated data) or V7 (exponent depends on training regime), these rows would read as support in that toy setting. Peer review status (NeurIPS) is taken from the record and not verifiable from the text.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test held-out pretraining cross-entropy in language models.
No small-run fits are used to predict much larger language-model runs.
The compute allocation is between linear-model size M and optimization steps L, not language-model parameters and token count; the study does not test the claimed parameter/token allocation trend.
Tests repeated-data training in sketched linear regression, not image/video models, LLMs, fine-tuning or transfer.
Tests a training-regime difference between one-pass and multi-pass SGD; does not vary parameter-count conventions, fitting method, or language-model training schedules and data.

relation.reason: The introduction, related work and conclusion discuss neural scaling laws and data reuse as motivation; the study's own results concern linear regression.

tranche.reason: The study derives and simulates population-MSE scaling for sketched linear regression. It does not test the neural-model claim versions or use their empirical findings as a tool.

source_check.notes: The theorem requires the stepsize assumptions of Theorem 3.1, including γ ≲ 1/log N. Section 4 identifies Figure 1(b) with constant-stepsize iterate averaging, but the caption assigns geometric decay to (b); R9 follows the narrative.

reader_labels.reason: The study derives power-law test-error bounds for multi-pass SGD, including data-constrained rates and simulations; see R1–R7, R9, R11, and R13–R14.

reader_labels.label: supports
